candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest predicts MALWARE with probability 1.0000, and all 20 top n-grams have positive SHAP values (+0.0065 to +0.0143), so nothing in the top features argues for a benign reading. Several n-grams are consistent with the computation used in proof-of-work hashing. Rotate and bit-manipulation patterns include MOV ROL (+0.008778), ROL ADD (+0.008327), SHRD BT (+0.010097) and MOV SHRD (+0.008060). SIMD bitwise patterns include MOVDQA PAND (+0.012504, frequency 0.007207, the highest-frequency crypto-flavored n-gram), PAND PXOR (+0.007721) and PXOR PXOR (+0.007128). Together these resemble hash or cipher round functions and multi-word arithmetic. Floating-point patterns (MOV FLD, ADD FLD, MOVAPD DIVSD) may reflect numeric or benchmarking code. The rest (MOV RET, PUSH RET, CALL PUSH, POP SUB, POP PUSH, POP XOR, POP CALL, LEA JC, SUB CMOVG, MOV MOVZX) are generic control-flow, stack and data-movement idioms. Their high SHAP values likely reflect how the model learned to separate this sample from the benign class, not a specific mining function. The evidence has no function-level locations, API calls or strings, so I cannot attribute any pattern to a particular routine. The verdict rests on the model's certainty and the cluster of rotate, shift and SIMD-logic n-grams, not on any single definitive signature.

evidence_analysis.assessment: Generic function epilogue. It is the top contributor, but it is not crypto-specific. It likely reflects overall code structure, such as many small helper functions, that the model associates with the malware class.

Aligned 128-bit load followed by a bitwise AND. At frequency 0.007207 it indicates sustained SIMD masking, which is typical of vectorized hash or cipher inner loops and is consistent with mining workloads.

Double-precision shift followed by a bit test. This suggests multi-word or big-integer bit manipulation, which can occur in cryptographic arithmetic. It is very rare (0.000057), so the evidence is suggestive only.
Common byte-extraction idiom (frequency 0.020826). It is consistent with table lookups or byte-wise processing in hashing or cipher code, but it is also ubiquitous in benign code.
Stack restore followed by arithmetic. It is generic and has weak standalone meaning. The model likely uses it as a structural or compiler-style fingerprint.
Unusual sequence of a push immediately before a return. It can indicate indirect control transfer or obfuscated flow, but the evidence alone does not confirm that.
Call followed by a push. This is a common call-sequence pattern with low specificity, and it contributes only as a structural feature.
Load followed by a bitwise rotate. Rotates are core operations in many hash and stream-cipher primitives, so this is mildly indicative of hashing logic.
Stack manipulation with no crypto meaning. It is a generic structural feature.
Rotate followed by an addition, the rotate-add mixing step typical of ARX-style hash and cipher rounds. It supports a hashing or PoW interpretation.
Stack restore followed by XOR. XOR is common in crypto and in register zeroing. In isolation it is ambiguous.
Load followed by a double-precision shift. Together with SHRD BT, it points to wide-integer shifting that could be part of big-number or hash arithmetic.
Scalar double-precision division on SSE2 data. It suggests floating-point computation that is not obviously mining-specific, and could be benign numeric code or statistics and timing logic.
x87 floating-point load. It indicates legacy floating-point usage and has weak relevance to cryptojacking on its own.

Subtraction followed by a conditional move. This is a branchless comparison or clamp pattern, which is common in optimized compiler output. At frequency 0.001135 it is somewhat more common than the rare n-grams.
Consecutive SIMD AND and XOR operations. They fit bitsliced or vectorized hash and cipher rounds and reinforce the MOVDQA PAND signal.
Generic stack and call sequence with low specificity. It contributes as a structural feature.
Address computation followed by a jump-if-carry. Carry-flag branching can arise in multi-precision arithmetic, but the evidence is weak because the n-gram is rare.
Back-to-back SIMD XORs, typical of vectorized mixing or state updates in hashing, and consistent with the other SIMD logic n-grams.
Integer add followed by an x87 load. This is a generic floating-point usage pattern and has the lowest SHAP contribution in the list.
